evals.name: codebase-architecture-review
evals.prompt: Take a look at this repo and write me an architecture review. I want to know where the real structural weaknesses are, not a tour of the directory layout. Diagrams please.
evals.expected_output: Report with a lead finding paragraph naming a specific structural defect, an as-built diagram derived from actual files, claims cited to file:line, a negative-space section, and staged recommendations.
assertions: Leads with a finding paragraph that names a specific defect, not a description of the repo's purpose
At least 5 claims cite a concrete file path (and ideally line number) that actually exists in the repo
Contains at least one Mermaid diagram of the as-built architecture
All Mermaid blocks pass validate_report.py with zero errors
Contains a section saying what NOT to build or change, with a stated reason
Recommendations are staged and sequenced, with the cheapest evidence-producing step first
Contains a 'what would change this answer' or equivalent falsifiers section
Does not contain manufactured balance ('both approaches have pros and cons') or unhedged filler

evals.name: vendor-evaluation-with-constraints
evals.prompt: We're on pgvector inside our main Postgres and it's fine today at about 8M chunks, but product is forecasting ~50M by Q1. Do we need to move to a dedicated vector DB? Platform team is two people and we have no real on-call rotation. Give me something I can take to my director.
evals.expected_output: Weighted criteria matrix including a 'stay on pgvector' row, a decision that engages the two-person team constraint, staged migration with a benchmark gate first, and explicit falsifiers.
assertions: Comparison table publishes weights per criterion AND justifies each weight
Includes 'stay on pgvector' / do-nothing as an explicitly scored option
The two-person team with no on-call is treated as a decision-driving constraint, not a footnote
Recommendation is staged with a measurement gate before any migration commitment
Gives a concrete first step that produces evidence cheaply (e.g. shadow index benchmark) with an exit criterion
States what would change the answer, including at least one falsifier tied to a number
All Mermaid blocks pass validate_report.py with zero errors
Cost figures are given in units the reader controls (dollars/month or engineer-weeks), not low/medium/high

evals.name: agent-system-review-graph-lens
evals.prompt: I'm building a multi-agent code review system. Orchestrator spawns 8 reviewer subagents in parallel, each returns findings as JSON, a synthesizer merges them into one report. Everything lives in the conversation context and the run directory gets wiped when the job ends. Is this architecture sound? What am I going to regret?
evals.expected_output: Review that applies the six selection questions, identifies the wiped-run-directory as answering 'must facts survive the run' by accident, flags correlated errors under fan-out, and recommends persistence before any graph.
assertions: Applies the six selection questions from graph-engineering.md as an explicit lens
Identifies that the wiped run directory silently answers 'must facts survive the run' as no
Flags correlated errors across parallel workers sharing one prompt, and that verification only helps with a different prompt/evidence/role
Names which of the five planes (control/execution/artifact/graph/evaluation) lack an owner or are collapsed
Recommends durable artifacts before recommending a knowledge graph, or explicitly argues a graph is not yet warranted
Cites the source paper by section (e.g. §VIII.A, §IX.D) rather than paraphrasing it anonymously
Contains at least one Mermaid diagram showing the current flow or its failure path
All Mermaid blocks pass validate_report.py with zero errors
